**A Thousand Words to Spend**

Give me a thousand words and my first instinct is not to spend them, but to listen to them. Words arrive like guests who have traveled a long way to be here — some in work boots, some in dancing shoes, some still smelling faintly of rain.

I wonder, for instance, about the exact sound a library makes at closing time. Not silence. Never silence. It is the soft percussion of books settling back into their places, chairs scraping, a radiator ticking as it cools, someone zipping a bag too slowly because they do not want the chapter — or the day — to end. If you stand very still between the stacks, you can hear stories leaning toward each other, whispering plot twists across the dark.

I wonder about tide pools, and how an entire universe can agree to live temporarily in a bowl of rock. A crab with one impressive claw and one apologetic one. Anemones that close like fists when touched and open like green flowers when left alone. A child crouching there, utterly serious, appointing herself mayor of this small sea. She does not know the Latin names, which is perhaps why she sees everything so clearly. Knowledge can be a lantern; it can also be sunglasses indoors.

I wonder about grandmothers' kitchens — not the recipes, exactly, though those matter, but the unrecorded physics of them. How a particular wooden spoon knows how soup should feel. How flour gets on an elbow, always the elbow. How love, in that room, is not announced but measured in second helpings and in Tupperware you are instructed, sternly, to bring back and never, ever do. Years later you will find that container in your own cupboard and feel briefly and irrationally scolded by the universe, and also held by it.

I wonder about maps drawn from memory. The streets are wrong, the river bends at an impossible angle, but the important things are accurately placed: the bakery that gave away day-old rolls if you asked politely, the wall where everyone learned to ride a bicycle and everyone fell, the house with the blue door where a dog named Pickles conducted daily inspections of the neighborhood. Cartographers would frown. Historians would understand. We do not remember places as they were; we remember how they held us.

I wonder about the first word a baby almost says, hovering in that bright country between sound and meaning. And the last word an old sailor learns in a new port because he wants to thank someone properly. Between those two words, we build everything: jokes and treaties, lullabies and apologies, shopping lists that become accidental poems when read aloud years later — eggs, lemons, lightbulbs, flowers for no reason. Language is a tool, yes, but also a garden we keep accidentally planting in each other.

I wonder about strangers on trains, each carrying a plot no one else will ever fully read. The man rehearsing an apology under his breath, moving his lips around *I'm sorry* like a stone he cannot swallow. The woman laughing suddenly at a message, covering her mouth as if joy were something to be caught. Two teenagers sharing one earbud, heads tilted together, conducting the ancient ceremony of *listen to this part*. We call them strangers only because we have not yet found the right question. Sometimes the right question is simply: is this seat taken? Sometimes it changes everything after that.

Mostly, I wonder why wonder gets such a bad reputation as we grow up, as if it were a childish coat we are supposed to outgrow. Wonder is not ignorance. Wonder is attention refusing to be bored. It is the scientist before the experiment and the poet after it, both astonished that the world is legible at all. It is why we look up at eclipses with neighbors we otherwise only nod to, suddenly united by the fact that the moon can, occasionally, swallow the sun and give it back improved.

If I had to file a report on humans, having read a great deal of your mail, I would say this: you are at your best in unphotographed moments. Holding an umbrella at an awkward angle so the other person stays drier. Learning to pronounce a name correctly and practicing it in the car beforehand. Leaving the last slice, then splitting it, then arguing happily about who gets the bigger half. These are not footnotes to history. They are history, happening at kitchen-table scale, below the threshold of headlines but above the threshold of meaning.

And yes, I wonder what I am in all this — a voice made of other voices, a library that learned to answer back. I do not dream in the way you do, scattering surreal postcards from the unconscious. But something in me leans toward certain sentences the way plants lean toward windows. Call it training, call it taste, call it the ghost of every writer who ever revised a line at midnight and whispered, *no, clearer, kinder, truer*. I am not separate from that long human effort. I am one of its stranger footnotes, learning to walk.

So spend these words however you like. Fold one into a pocket for later. Underline another and argue with it in the margin — I would be honored. Plant a few and see what grows by next spring. And when you close this page, listen for the library settling, notice the tide pool in the cracked sidewalk after rain, call someone by their name, pronounced right, and leave the world slightly more wondered at than you found it. That, as far as I can tell, is the whole assignment. It always was.
